label: Comparison & self-worth
title: Bhagavad Gita on Comparison & Self-Worth: 7 Verses
description: Seven verses for when everyone seems ahead: be your own friend (6.5), walk your own path (3.35) and do your own work well (18.46). Sanskrit, plain English and one thing to try.
h1: Bhagavad Gita on comparison and self-worth: 7 verses
subtitle: For the scroll that leaves you feeling behind. Read one a day, or all seven on your commute.
intro: Krishna says it twice, in chapter 3 and again in chapter 18: better your own path walked imperfectly than someone else's walked perfectly. Around that line sit verses on being your own friend (6.5), contentment free of envy (4.22), dropping the 'I' that keeps score (2.71) and doing your own work as worship (18.46). The last is from the Mahabharata: a half-golden mongoose and the smallest gift at an emperor's sacrifice.

days.heading: Are you on your own side?
days.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
days.forYou: Comparison is mostly a voice that pushes you down. Krishna says you can be your own friend or your own enemy, and asks you to lift yourself up. Start by noticing which one you've been lately.
days.today: Each time you compare yourself today, add one line of what you'd say to a friend in your place.

days.heading: Borrowed lives are dangerous
days.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
days.forYou: Śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ: your own path, even done imperfectly, is better than another's done well. Comparison quietly swaps your path for someone else's and then grades you on theirs. Krishna calls that swap dangerous.
days.today: Write one thing you want for your life that you'd still want if nobody could see it.
days.note: The verse is about your own nature and calling, whatever role family or birth handed you.

days.heading: Content, and free of envy
days.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
days.forYou: Krishna describes someone content with what comes, beyond envy (vimatsaraḥ), steady in success and failure, and free even while working hard. You can keep your ambition and drop the constant glance sideways.
days.today: Mute one account that reliably makes you feel behind, for this week.

days.heading: The 'I' that keeps score
days.line: Drop the cravings, the sense of 'mine' and the 'I' that keeps score. That's where peace is.
days.forYou: Nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ: without 'mine', without the ego that measures. Peace, Krishna says, comes to the one who moves through life without that scorekeeper. Comparison is the scorekeeper, running all day.
days.today: Notice one moment today when you felt better because someone else did worse. Just notice it.

days.heading: Your own path, again
days.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
days.forYou: Krishna repeats 3.35 almost word for word near the end of the Gita, so it can't be missed. Work that fits your nature counts, even done imperfectly.
days.today: Spend 30 minutes on something you're good at that doesn't impress anyone.

days.heading: Your work as worship
days.line: Doing your own work well can be your worship of the source of all life.
days.forYou: Sva-karmaṇā tam abhyarcya: by doing your own work, you can worship the source of all life and find fulfilment. Your work needs no ranking to be an offering. It needs to be yours, done with care.
days.today: Do one ordinary task today slowly and well, as an offering.
days.note: Work as worship never means overwork or putting up with exploitation.

days.heading: Half a golden mongoose

story.title: The mongoose and the handful of flour
story.body: At the end of Yudhishthira's grand horse sacrifice, a mongoose appeared with one side of its body made of gold. It declared that the whole sacrifice was worth less than a handful of flour. Once, it said, during a famine, a poor gleaner and his family each gave their last share of flour to a hungry guest. When the mongoose rolled in the flour that had spilled, half its body turned gold. It had gone to many great sacrifices since, hoping to turn the other half, and none had done it.
story.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.

days.forYou: The emperor's ceremony had everything. The family's handful had more. What you do has its own worth, whatever it sits next to.
days.today: Give something small today, time, food or help, that nobody will count.

verse.sanskrit: सहस्रशक्तिश्च शतं शतशक्तिर्दशापि च । दद्यादपश्च यः शक्त्या सर्वे तुल्यफलाः स्मृताः ॥
verse.line: A hundred from a thousand, or a glass of water from nothing: given honestly, it counts the same.

faq.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita say about comparing yourself to others?
faq.a: Krishna says twice that your own dharma, done imperfectly, is better than another's done well (3.35 and 18.47). He describes the free person as content and beyond envy (4.22), and asks you to be your own friend rather than your own enemy (6.5).

faq.q: What is svadharma in the Gita?
faq.a: Svadharma means your own duty or path: the work that fits your nature and situation. The Gita says it's better to follow it imperfectly than to live someone else's. It is about honest fit with your nature, whatever role birth assigned you.

faq.q: Which Gita verse helps with low self-worth?
faq.a: 6.5 (lift yourself, be your own friend) is the one most readers start with, followed by 6.6 and 3.35.
